articles.title_orig: China’s plenum backs tighter party discipline, a priority for Xi. Here's why it matters
articles.title_zh: China’s plenum backs tighter party discipline, a priority for Xi. Here's why it matters
articles.content_orig:
This is the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300
A record 33 members have been expelled from China's Communist Party as it concluded a major annual political gathering, which had the most empty seats ever seen.
The fifth plenum was attended by 279 Central Committee members, compared to 315 at the fourth plenum in October 2025 and 364 at the third one in July 2024.
While recent plenums focused on economic reforms or social and development issues, party discipline took centre stage at this week's gathering.
Xi Jinping has made the fight against corruption a central pillar of his rule since he took the reins in 2012, calling it the "biggest threat" to the party.
Since then, more than two million individuals have been disciplined for cases related to "pointless formalities, bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance", Zhang Fuhai, from the party's disciplinary commission, told a press briefing on Friday.
He also said the party would enhance its efforts to ensure officials "dare not, cannot, and do not want to be corrupt".
Sixteen of the 33 members expelled are from the military, according to a communique issued on Thursday, which marked the end of the four-day closed-door gathering held at a hotel in Beijing.
It's unclear what specific charges these members face beyond "serious disciplinary and legal violations". Such broad allegations have become routine under Xi's anti-corruption campaign.
It has now become "an effort to consolidate and maintain authority", says Chong Ja Ian, a non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
"In this case, the campaign will continue and expand depending on how secure Xi feels rather than any real issue with corruption."
In its statement, the party said it has "squarely confronted the grim reality that party leadership had at times weakened or hollowed out" and that it will continue to "enforce strict party self-governance, including turning the knife inwards to... curb disorder".
The latest expulsions bring the total number of members removed under Xi's third term to a record 51, up from 35 and five in his first and second terms respectively.
Beyond the plenum, China's top anti-corruption watchdog reported that 680,000 people across the party apparatus have been disciplined in the first nine months of this year.
This is also the first time in Xi's 14 years of leadership that plenum attendance fell below 300. The current Central Committee started its term in 2022 with more than 370 members.
Observers argue that Xi views corruption not just as graft but also ideological impurity and, crucially, disloyalty.
In January, he warned against "two-faced cadres" who profess political loyalty but defy orders and act in their self-interest.
The party says it's going after "pointless formalities", which inlcude "bureaucratism, hedonism and extravagance"
Among the high-ranking officials expelled are former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui, and ex-top generals Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli. Official statements announcing their removal this year said they "seriously violated [the party's] discipline and rules", which is widely read as a euphemism for corruption.
The culling of the military's top brass has been particularly significant, with Neil Thomas, Lobsang Tsering and Shengyu Wang from the Asia Society Policy Institute describing it as "in a category of its own".
"It raises serious questions about organisational leadership and combat readiness, even as China continues to unveil formidable new military hardware," they wrote.
Zhang was also vice-chairman of the Central Military Commission, which controls the armed forces. The seven-member commission has since been whittled down to just two members: Xi as chairman and Zhang Shengmin vice-chairman.
Ma and Zhang Youxia were former Politburo members. Their removal, along with former general He Weidong in 2025, meant the powerful 24-man Politburo was at one point left with 21 members.
Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the top decision-making body at the fifth plenum, bringing the number to 22.
Former prominent diplomat Liu Jianchao, who disappeared from public view in July last year, was also named among those who have been purged.
"Xi has few qualms about removing people he promoted," Chong says. "That he does so at will with little opposition underscores how unassailable his position is at the moment."
Analysts believe one reason for the increased emphasis on discipline â which many interpret as loyalty â is next year's Party Congress, when the CCP will vote again for its next leader.
A leadership reshuffle is due in 2027 and many analysts expect Xi to hold on to the top job for a fourth term and beyond. No leader has served that long except Mao Zedong, the founder of Communist China.
Xi has reason to "scrutinise the next cohort more closely" given the fall of so many officials from the current committee, Thomas says.
"Today's rising stars tend to be relatively young, boast technocratic backgrounds, and have connections to Xi's political network," he says, adding that "provincial leadership ranks are a promising place to look".
Observers say that ultimately, Xi is expected to dominate personnel selection at the 21st Party Congress, which will further cement his grip on the party and the country.
"Xi's focus is further consolidating power around himself... The readout from the plenum suggests he intends to be at the centre of China and the Communist Party for the foreseeable future," Chong says.
"However, further down the road, such concentration of power may pave the way for a more serious power vacuum when Xi ages and slows down."
'Tigers and flies': Millions of officials later, why is Xi's corruption purge still going?

articles.title_orig: Stock Market News, Oct. 30, 2026: Tech Selloff Pushes Nasdaq to Its Worst Month in Over a Year
articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, Oct. 30, 2026: Tech Selloff Pushes Nasdaq to Its Worst Month in Over a Year
articles.content_orig:
Worries are rising about whether hundreds of billions of dollars in AI investment will produce enough profit and productivity to be worth it
A sell-off for tech stocks got even worse on Friday on worries that Wall Street’s frenzy around artificial intelligence technology sent prices too high.
The S&P 500 tumbled 1.8 per cent for its worst day since June, and it closed out a third straight losing week. The weakness for technology stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down a market-leading 2.9 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572 points, or 1.1 per cent.
The US stock market remains only 3.1 per cent below its all-time high, which has boosted the value of workers’ 401(k) accounts, but it has become increasingly shaky as Tuesday’s midterm elections in the US approach.

articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protestors and groups of police charging to disperse protestors in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_orig: Poland deploys riot police, as court chief’s ousting sparks crisis
articles.title_zh: Poland deploys riot police, as court chief’s ousting sparks crisis
articles.content_orig:
President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, returning to Warsaw to deal with the turmoil at home
Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, as riot police deployed around the country’s constitutional court on Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested against the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski.
The court’s official social media account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and some demonstrators chanted “Tusk traitor”, as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

articles.title_orig: Trump says US looking into Binance hack: ‘We don’t know’ if North Korea responsible
articles.title_zh: Trump says US looking into Binance hack: ‘We don’t know’ if North Korea responsible
articles.content_orig:
Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, has suspended withdrawals after hackers broke into its digital wallets and stole $6 billion in what appears to be the biggest crypto heist ever.
The exchange said Friday that it has begun recovering affected assets and was continuing to work with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms to trace additional funds.
An initial investigation suggested the hack went through an engineer’s laptop, “which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions,” Binance said late on Thursday. Blockchain evidence suggests the hack originated in North Korea, according to multiple crypto-tracing firms.
A team of cryptocurrency firms managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen loot amid a frenetic battle with the hackers to find and control the digital money.
Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said on X that the attack was not a “one-click” action, but rather a complex process. The investigation has not attributed responsibility to any individual nor found evidence of any wallet private key leak.
Binance said it would cover all losses from the company’s funds and an emergency assets fund, adding “user funds are safe.” The crypto exchange said it had temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals to allow security checks to be completed and blockchain intelligence partners to trace and recover funds. The crypto exchange expects withdrawal services to resume by Sunday morning.
Crypto-tracing firm TRM Labs attributed the heist to an elite North Korean hacking unit “based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” pointing out that “several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists.”
Pangolin Intelligence, another blockchain-tracking firm based in Singapore, said it also believed that a North Korean hacking unit was behind the heist.
“Analyzing the on-chain activity related to this hack and correlating with information gathered from previous known incidents” led to the attribution, said an analyst with Pangolin Intelligence, who did not want to be named for privacy reasons.
“I think the cat and mouse game has barely begun yet,” the Pangolin Intelligence analyst told CNN, adding that North Korea was likely poised to tap a network of money laundering organizations to try to cash out the stolen funds.
Chainalysis, another crypto-tracking company, said it was monitoring stolen funds “moving across multiple blockchains,” including bitcoin and ethereum. A Chainalysis spokesperson told CNN the firm had “high confidence” North Korea was behind the hack.
CNN has reached out to North Korea’s mission at the UN for comment. Pyongyang has previously denied hacking allegations.
In past investigations of big crypto hacks, the FBI has had an on-call team of analysts that worked to freeze some of the money.
The FBI said in a statement Friday that it is “aware of the incident and is engaged with relevant public and private partners to understand the scope of the activity, evaluate potential impacts, and coordinate appropriate investigative steps.”
A spokesperson for the US Secret Service, which also investigates cybercrime, said the agency’s “investigators are working around the clock with our private-sector partners, including Circle [the company behind the US dollar-backed stablecoin USDC], to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds stolen from Binance on Thursday. We are also coordinating closely with the United States Attorney’s Office for the District of Columbia and law enforcement partners to identify the cyber criminals responsible and bring them to justice.”
If North Korea is proven to be the culprit, it would be little surprise to US law enforcement officials and private experts. North Korean hackers were blamed for the previous record-high crypto hack, when they allegedly stole $1.5 billion from Bybit, another major cryptocurrency exchange. In that case, the attackers stole an amount equal to a significant portion of North Korea’s reported annual gross domestic product in a matter of minutes.
North Korea’s formidable hacking teams are a key source of revenue for the nuclear-armed, sanctions-battered regime, according to current and former US and South Korean officials. Pyongyang-linked hackers have stolen billions of dollars from banks and cryptocurrency firms in the last several years, according to reports from the United Nations and private firms.
A 2023 CNN investigation spotlighted how the South Korean intelligence service worked with private crypto-tracking experts to seize about $1 million in cryptocurrency that North Koreans had stolen from a victim.
Inside the international sting operation to catch North Korean crypto hackers
Unlike platforms for trading stocks, cryptocurrency exchanges tend to hold digital assets on their users’ behalf, which make them more vulnerable to hackers and theft, particularly given a lack of regulatory oversight within the relatively nascent industry.
Binance was co-founded in 2017 by Canadian national Changpeng Zhao, becoming the world’s largest crypto trading platform within a year of its launch.
However, Zhao stepped down in 2023 after pleading guilty to violating anti-money laundering laws in the US. He was sentenced to four months in federal prison, and was pardoned by President Donald Trump in October last year.
Zhao, who no longer manages the platform but remains its largest shareholder, said on X that he expects user funds to be fully covered by the exchange, pushing back against any suggestion to the contrary in a spat on X with Elon Musk.
Prices of bitcoin and ether, the most widely traded cryptocurrencies, plummeted following news of the Binance breach, but regained some losses to trade about 2-3% lower midday Friday in Hong Kong.
This story has been updated.

articles.title_orig: Sutter promised a $1 billion new hospital in the East Bay. Now, it’s pulling the plug
articles.title_zh: Sutter promised a $1 billion new hospital in the East Bay. Now, it’s pulling the plug
articles.content_orig:
Election 2026: Berkeley and Alameda County voter guide and news
When Sutter Health announced plans to build a new hospital and medical campus in Emeryville last year, Berkeley officials hailed the development as a way to ensure residents would still have an emergency room and other inpatient services nearby after the impending closure of Alta Bates hospital.
Now the Sacramento health giant is scrapping that plan.
Sutter officials announced Friday that they will build only outpatient services at the Emeryville site, while seeking another location for a new full-service hospital. The company also plans to push for changes to state law that would postpone the closure of its Alta Bates campus until the new facility opens.
“We remain committed to building a new hospital in the East Bay and are evaluating potential sites that can support emergency care, advanced clinical services and the region’s future needs,” Sutter President and CEO Warner Thomas and Executive Vice President and Chief Operating Officer Christina Oh wrote in a joint statement Friday.
State Sen. Jesse Arreguín criticized the decision in a statement.
“Sutter is walking away from its commitment to build a new hospital in Emeryville, and our communities will pay the price,” Arreguín wrote. “I am calling on Sutter to choose people over profits. I will not accept leaving the East Bay without the hospital capacity our communities need, and I will keep fighting for a full-service hospital and the critical care East Bay residents deserve.”
Alta Bates has been slated for closure since 2016, with Sutter officials saying the building is out of compliance with state earthquake safety regulations that go into effect in 2030. The company planned to move inpatient services to its Oakland campus .
The move to close Alta Bates sparked concern from local officials and labor groups because it would leave only a single full-service hospital, a Kaiser facility in Richmond, in the area between the Carquinez Strait and the Sutter and Kaiser campuses in Oakland. Sutter appeared to put those concerns to rest with the plans it revealed in early 2025 to spend upwards of $1 billion on a new 200-bed hospital — complete with emergency room, labor and delivery facilities and intensive care — at the intersection of Hollis and 53rd Street in Emeryville.
In their statement Friday, Sutter officials wrote that the hospital project was vulnerable to a legal challenge under the California Environmental Quality Act that could have caused years of delays to construction.
Sutter sought what it described as “relief” from the powerful environmental law through state legislation, but those efforts didn’t deliver the assurance the company wanted to move forward with the Emeryville project. The San Francisco Chronicle reported Friday that state lawmakers considered a bill to streamline approval for that project and another hospital Sutter plans to build in Santa Clara, but removed the Emeryville project without explanation before passing the law this summer.
“We cannot allow that uncertainty to stall needed investments in care,” Thomas and Oh wrote.
Arreguín’s statement did not address the streamlining bill, and instead accused Sutter of providing “shifting explanations” for why the project won’t move forward.
“East Bay residents deserve transparency and a real plan,” Arreguín wrote.
Sutter officials did not say what other locations in the East Bay are under consideration for the new hospital.

articles.title_orig: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
articles.title_zh: King visits Guyanese slave rebellion site on Caribbean tour
articles.content_orig:
The King has made a poignant visit to the site where a Guyanese slave rebellion was violently resisted by British authorities, making the stop during his tour of the Caribbean.
He visited Independence Park in Georgetown to remember the Demerera Slave Rebellion of 1823, which saw an uprising by thousands of enslaved people.
Accompanied by Guyana's Culture Minister, Steven Jacobs, he was told how hundreds of slaves were killed by colonial leaders during the rebellion and many of those who survived were executed close to where the King stood.
Above the King was a sign that he took time to read.
"This ground was used as a public execution site," it said, "where enslaved persons...were condemned to death and hung."
The moment of reflection was what Buckingham Palace had described as the King "not shying away from the UK's colonial legacy" and described today as a chance for the King to reflect on Guyana's history of slavery and resistance.
In 2022, Charles described how he was on a personal journey of discovery and was continuing to "deepen my own understanding of slavery's enduring impact", in a speech at the opening of a Commonwealth summit hosted by Rwanda .
Independence Park, which is now a sports ground, drew a crowd of dozens of schoolchildren. The King stopped to talk to many of them asking them about their homework, their holidays and if they'd had a day off school.
Outside one of the King's engagements later in the day, a small but noisy group of protesters gathered.
Many held placards saying "no apology will return what was stolen, reparations now" and "justice must not depend on wealth status and connections".
"This great wealth was built on the backs of slavery," said protester, Guyanese politician, Terrence Campbell.
"I do not want the British public to think that by me saying reparations can take various forms, it means that they do not have responsibility for reparations. They do, because the United Kingdom benefited tremendously from slavery."
The King will not be apologising for the UK involvement in the slave trade during the visit, nor will he offer reparations - compensation from those countries who benefited from the slave trade - in line with the position of the UK government.
This tour has seen a number of demonstrations so far but none have seriously disrupted the King's programme.
Royal tours often include cultural exchanges and the King's trip to Guyana saw an unusual mix up of musical styles.
On the bandstand of Promenade Gardens in Georgetown, the bagpipes of the National Piping Centre could be heard alongside traditional Guyanese drummers in a collaboration of musical styles.
Seven pipers from the National Piping Centre have been touring Guyana over the past week to learn more about the Guyanese musical traditions.
As part of his visit on Friday, the King also shared a moment with a veterans from Guyana who fought for Britain in the Second World War during an event at the Commonwealth War Graves in the capital Georgetown.
King Charles met Donald Grant, 99, who will celebrate his 100th birthday next week on November 3.
He also spoke to James Samuel, 100, who is in a wheelchair, with the the King hearing how aged 19 he enlisted in the British Guiana Volunteer Force in 1943.
"What a great pleasure it is to see you on this occasion," the King told him.
The King was waved off at the end of his state visit by Britain's High Commissioner to Guyana, Joseph Fisher, Guyana's Prime Minister Mark Phillips and a number of other dignitaries.
His departure had a small ceremonial element with the Guyana Defence Force providing a guard of honour at Cheddi Jagan International Airport.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.title_zh: Anthropic orders AI tool Claude to stop remaking video games
articles.content_orig:
Update: Anthropic has confirmed it's released an update to Opus 5.5 to "steer" Claude Code away from "recreating someone else's specific game."
It appears Anthropic may be (quietly) taking action to stem the flood of AI-driven game remakes that have hit the video game industry in the last few month, which saw users creating their own versions of classic and upcoming games, sometimes for fun, sometimes for financial gain.
Earlier today X (formerly Twitter) user Chasm said that they spotted an update to Claude Code's "rules" that was pushed sometime on October 27. The rule is listed under "tengu_heron_brook," and reads "Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Do not build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original." Chasm reports that there is no way to disable the rule.
An Anthropic spokesperson referred us to a statement by Anthropic member of technical staff Addy Osmani also posted on X. "We added two sentences to Claude Code's prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else's specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy," Osmani wrote. "Original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets are meant to keep working. We'll continue to iterate to ensure we're striking the right balance."
Related: GDC Side Quest - An anti-cheat primer with Lucia Suarez
"In the meantime, if Claude turns down something that's yours, send it my way."
Fear over the potential of fast-follow AI remakes that might beat the copied game to market has spread among independent developers in the last few weeks. Digital Sun Games is one of several studios to cancel their upcoming public playtest for fear someone might ingest the demo into an AI tool and release their own version of its upcoming game ReVamp . Developers have also pressed Valve to explain how it can prevent the shady clones from supplanting their games on Steam, prompting the company to offer a rare explanation to developers in South Korea earlier in this week .
While developers may take some relief that Anthropic at least doesn't want to actively encourage mass game copying, this rule may only deter the most low-effort copycats. Scientists and reporters have repeatedly documented that safety limits on generative AI tools can be sidestepped by deploying rhetorical tricks . It's also unclear how the software would be able to interpret whether or not a user owns a game idea or game assets.
And as many users responding to Chasm pointed out, if Claude becomes too difficult to use, vibe-coding cloners can turn to open-weight models that have no such restrictions in place.
GameDeveloper.com has reached out to Anthropic for comment and will update this story upon its response.
Related: Epic VP says AI code tools have stomped out decade-old 'non-deterministic cooking bugs' in Unreal Engine
Update 10/30: This story has been updated with confirmation from Anthropic.
Senior Editor, GameDeveloper.com
Bryant Francis is a writer, journalist, and narrative designer based in Boston, MA. He currently writes for Game Developer, a leading B2B publication for the video game industry. His credits include Proxy Studios' 4X strategy game Zephon, Iron Anchor Studios' Down With The Ship, and Amplitude Studio's 2017 game Endless Space 2.

articles.title_orig: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.title_zh: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.content_orig:
In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers this week, and later obtained by MacRumors , Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue.
If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance.
Apple's memo said the issue affects a small number of iPhone Duo units, which is consistent with what it said in a public statement on Monday.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," said Apple, in a statement shared with MacRumors . If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." You can get support on Apple's website or by calling 1-800-APL-CARE in the U.S. and Canada.
Apple said most iPhone Duo units are not susceptible to this issue and that impacted units appear to exhibit the defects rather quickly after usage.
Apple said there is no iPhone Duo recall, and the company has yet to launch a public-facing repair program on its website for this issue.
Almost immediately after the iPhone Duo began arriving to customers a week ago, a handful of early adopters reported that the device's inner display had cracked , resulting in lines appearing down the middle and towards the right side of the screen.
The electronics repair website iFixit completed an iPhone Duo teardown and said that the issue is likely related to a defective hinge on affected units. However, Apple has yet to comment on the underlying cause of the issue.

articles.title_zh: China Scoops Up Data That Could Aid Its Forces in Waters Around Taiwan
articles.content_orig:
Recent Chinese naval activity beyond the First Island Chain reflects the Chinese People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA) ability to conduct coordinated operations across the western Pacific and signals Beijing’s strategic ambitions, analysts said yesterday.
The assessment follows reports of Chinese naval movements stretching from southern Japan to Taiwan and the Philippines, reported separately by National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) and by Japan’s Joint Staff Office.
Lin Ying-yu (林穎佑), an associate professor at Tamkang University’s Graduate Institute of International Affairs and Strategic Studies, said the PLA had integrated naval forces from its northern, eastern and southern theater commands.
Its naval operations should be viewed not as separate activities by individual theater commands, but as part of a broader “First Island Chain theater,” with interconnected vessel movements reflecting an overall operational plan for the First Island Chain, he said.
Citing information from Japan’s Joint Staff Office, Lin said the Liaoning aircraft carrier strike group passed through the Miyako Strait and sailed east of Taiwan toward the Philippine Sea.
The movement indicated that China’s focus remained on the South China Sea, where Beijing was using a form of “gunboat diplomacy” to pressure Manila, Lin said.
Lin said the attention on China’s aircraft carrier should not overshadow other advanced warships, particularly the Type 055 guided-missile destroyer seen in the operation, which he described as a measure of the Chinese navy’s combat strength.
Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌), an associate research fellow at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, said that PLA Navy activity had three political implications.
The activity was a response to the US-Japan Keen Sword 27 exercise, held on Monday last week to yesterday on Japan’s southwestern islands, and to a Wednesday meeting in Cebu between US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and Japanese Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi, Shu said.
The two officials agreed to strengthen defense cooperation along the First Island Chain linking Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines, he said.
Shu added that the naval activity was also a response to a US Army guide calling for regional forces to mobilize on the first day of an Indo-Pacific conflict and identifying China as a “pacing threat.”
On the military front, Shu said the Liaoning aircraft carrier is deployed at sea annually, but the scale of China’s naval forces involved this time was significant.
He said China was using routine exercises to build its ability to operate beyond the First Island Chain and gradually develop carrier strike group capabilities modeled on the US Navy.

Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.
The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.
Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.
TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.
Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors .
Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry .

articles.title_orig: The Galaxy S27 Ultra chipset saga continues, here's the latest twist - GSMArena.com news
articles.title_zh: The Galaxy S27 Ultra chipset saga continues, here's the latest twist - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
Which chipset the Galaxy S27 Ultra will use has turned into quite the saga over the past few months. Back in July, the Ultra was said to be getting a Snapdragon chip globally , while the rest of the lineup would use the Exynos 2700 outside of North America. Then in early September, insiders claimed that Samsung was building Exynos 2700-powered S27 Ultras for Korea and Europe.
In early October, Samsung reportedly started mass producing the Exynos 2700 , with the decision for the Ultra still up in the air, and a few days later a new insider tip claimed that the S27 Ultra would only be available with a Qualcomm chipset . The middle of the month brought a report that the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 was running too hot in Samsung's testing , which Qualcomm promptly denied . And just last week, the Exynos 2700 reportedly beat Qualcomm's chip in internal tests once again.
Today, Ice Universe has chimed in with the latest installment, saying that so far there are still no signs of the Galaxy S27 Ultra using the Exynos 2700 in Europe. South Korea, on the other hand, remains uncertain, according to the tipster.
If that's right, European buyers will get the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 in their S27 Ultras, while the Korean model could still go either way. Obviously, nothing is final until Samsung makes it official, and judging by how this saga has gone so far, we wouldn't be surprised to see another twist or two before then.

Australia’s preparations for a possible conflict with China reflect “a relatively superficial understanding”, argues prominent economist John Edwards. Europe, Canada, Indonesia, Malaysia and India, he notes, are not preparing for such a conflict. Why should Australia?

articles.title_zh: Cracks are emerging in the AI spending boom
articles.content_orig:

Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.
Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.
Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.
The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.
A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.
Meanwhile, the wild success of AI Mode — Google’s AI-powered chatbot feature built directly into Search — is eating into the company’s money-maker. Google’s Search advertising business, which makes up roughly half of its revenue, saw growth slow to 12%, its weakest pace in five quarters. That leaves Google walking a tightrope. It’s spending billions on the AI technology that could undermine the search business that pays it.
Amazon is in a similar boat after reporting negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the past 12 months, compared with $14.8 billion in positive free cash flow the year before. The company says it expects to spend $220 billion in capex this year. Even though revenue at its cloud business, AWS, grew 39%, Amazon’s stock tumbled 7% after it reported earnings Thursday.
Meta is also burning cash, reporting negative free cash flow of $2.1 billion in the third quarter as capex outpaced its operating cash. It’s guiding to as much as $145 billion in capex this year. The company noted that Muse, its new free personal AI agent, is a bit of a money pit (it’s “very compute-intensive to run,” CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said). But ad revenue grew 26%. Still, no amount of good news saved Meta from taking a 10% hit on its stock last week.
Microsoft was the only exception when it came to free cash flow — it recorded $18.6 billion in positive free cash flow in its latest quarter, with spending on capex at $45.2 billion, less than the $50 billion it projected. Microsoft said that wasn’t an intentional pullback from AI spending, blaming delays in capacity from third-party providers. As a result, shares of smaller companies that rent out AI computing power sank .
It’s worth noting that the money to pay for all of this AI infrastructure isn’t just coming from the Big Tech companies’ profits. It’s also showing up in stock and bond sales. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle raised a combined $326 billion in debt in 2026, triple the amount raised last year.
Demand for AI compute remains strong. Google, Amazon, and Microsoft all saw gains in their cloud businesses. But investors are getting spooked by the costs of meeting that demand.
These muddied waters could complicate Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO. The AI company filed to go public earlier this week, and its future growth depends on securing enormous amounts of compute. Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone has warned investors the company might not qualify for an investment-grade rating after its IPO, meaning it might end up being more reliant on the hyperscalers and third-parties to fund its infrastructure ambitions.

articles.title_orig: Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court
articles.title_zh: Tusk-Nawrocki battle escalates as chief judge is ousted from Poland’s top court
articles.content_orig:
Poland’s constitutional court descended into turmoil Friday evening as judges barred from hearing cases moved to oust the institution’s nationalist-linked leadership, sparking accusations of a coup and tense protests.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge with the court, ordered its president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy to be suspended for a month and announced she was taking charge . Święczkowski rejected her authority , accusing those involved of a “coup d’état,” while his deputy was turned away at the building’s gates.
The showdown marks an escalation in Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s struggle to undo the judicial overhaul carried out by the nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) former government. During its eight years in power, PiS filled the Constitutional Tribunal with its appointees, including Święczkowski and his deputy, placing it at the heart of Poland’s confrontation with Brussels over the rule of law.
Outside the tribunal, protesters clashed with police , who said objects had been thrown at officers and three people detained after climbing over the court’s fence. Police said they had deployed to maintain security following warnings of threats to judges and staff, but had not entered the building.
PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński took part in the protest and tried to force his way into the court building. He accused Tusk of staging a “coup” against the court and turning Poland into a “police state,” and demanded presidential intervention.
President Karol Nawrocki, a PiS ally and rival of Tusk, interrupted his official trip to Senegal, declaring , “At a moment like this, the president must be in Poland.”
Tusk was defiant. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he wrote on X . “After years of PiS lawlessness, it’s a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
The tribunal, which can strike down legislation, helped impose a near-total abortion ban under PiS and challenged the supremacy of EU law . Last December, the EU’s top court ruled that it failed to meet European standards of judicial independence.
But efforts to change the court’s makeup have met resistance. Nawrocki refused to swear in five judges elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority. They took their oaths in parliament instead, but Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the turmoil on Święczkowski, who he accused of turning the institution into his “private fiefdom” and preventing newly elected judges from doing their jobs.
“And now the judges have spoken,” Żurek told POLITICO.
Żurek, who also serves as Poland’s prosecutor general, said he submitted five requests to lift the immunity of Święczkowski and his deputy, backed by 50 volumes of case files. He defended Korwin-Piotrowska’s move as a decision by a legally appointed judge, insisting that the government had nothing to do with it.

articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline, as an early recovery gave way to heavy selling after the Federal Reserve maintained its hawkish stance, stronger U.S. economic data reinforced expectations for further tightening, and Friday's technology-led equity rout triggered widespread liquidation across precious metals.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $3,994.95 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal initially pushed higher as bargain-hunting emerged following the previous week's selloff below $4,000. The recovery gathered momentum Tuesday as Treasury yields eased and the U.S. dollar softened, carrying gold back above $4,050 ahead of Wednesday's Federal Reserve policy decision. After the Fed voted 10-2 to hold interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two policymakers dissenting in favor of another 25-basis-point hike, spot prices ultimately set their weekly high at $4,082.50 per ounce just before the equity close on Wednesday, before sellers regained control.
Gold came under renewed pressure Thursday after stronger-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth and elevated core PCE inflation reinforced expectations that further monetary tightening could be necessary. The metal slipped back toward $4,000 as the dollar remained supported, despite some relief from easing Treasury yields and lower oil prices.
Selling accelerated dramatically on Friday as a sharp decline in technology stocks, driven by growing concerns over returns on artificial intelligence investment, triggered broader market liquidations. Gold broke decisively below $4,000 and continued falling alongside silver and other precious metals, as forced selling and expectations for another Fed rate hike overwhelmed safe-haven demand. Spot gold ultimately set its weekly low of $3,870.25 per ounce late Friday afternoon – its weakest level in more than a year – and was trading only a few dollars above that level heading into the close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street bulls abandoning ship after gold sank below $3,900, while Main Street maintained a narrow bullish majority bias despite the yellow metal’s price rout.
“Gold’s shine has dulled,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “The yellow metal was near $4700 as recently as late August. The one caveat is that the once-more precious metal is below the lower Bollinger Band (two standard deviations below the 20-day moving average. Still, there does not appear to have been a capitulation trade, and assuming a push to new lows for the year, I suspect gold can fall into the $3750-$3850 range.”
“Lower,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “It's a big week with the midterms and the potential resumption of the Iran war, but I fear that Trump could lash out and escalate, leading to a severe risk-off trade.”
“I am bearish on Gold for the coming week,” said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. “Technically, the breakdown below $4,000 is significant.”
“Unchanged,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “I see competing influences this coming week. Renewed strikes on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz may bring retaliation soon after U.S. mid-term elections. That should push oil prices higher and stoke inflation concerns… putting downward pressure on gold. But if Democrats make gains in the mid-term elections, it may very well drive uneasy Republicans to the safety and protection of gold.”
“I would treat every drop in gold prices as an opportunity to buy well,” Checkan added.
Daniel Pavilonis, senior commodities broker at StoneX Group, told Kitco News that now that gold and silver have broken near-term critical support, the precious metals may be in for a longer and deeper correction, and gold will need some indication of easing monetary policy to resume the upward trajectory of the last couple of years.
“We're still seeing some inflation,” he said. “We're seeing equities sell off. We're seeing commodities have come off, except for some of the energy sector.
Pavilonis said the market is in the midst of an unwind. “If you're looking at the charts, they don't look so hot... If you're just looking at this from a technical standpoint, not any fundamentals, it looks like we could go lower.”
As for how low the precious metals could slide, Pavilonis said the metals could be in for a deep pullback before sustained buying resumes.
“I could see silver getting as low as the high $30s,” he said. “I could see gold getting as low as somewhere around $3,000. I think it's very likely to happen into the first quarter of next year, and then maybe just base out for a little while, and then possibly move higher.”
Pavilonis said he’s seen this time and time again. “What happened the last few times when silver hit $50, when gold spikes up? We sell off afterward,” he said. “The party is over. The themes that we [saw at the early 2026 highs], the same headlines, the same stories… because of inflation, because of this or that. People need to rationalize why it went up so much. But if you go back into the archives and look at news around 1980 – before people realized it was the Hunt brothers, which was part of the story – but it was the same thing: ‘We're running out of silver, we're running out of gold, the exchanges are low, warehouses are low, inventories… And people are buying, and so you’ve got to go out and buy some gold, go out and buy some silver!’ There were almost identical New York Times articles being written about silver and gold in the run-up to 1980.”
“Now I think that anybody from the move to the upside that hasn't been stopped out, or is holding on the physical side, It's time to hedge,” he said. “You want to start collaring around positions. You want to start collaring and capitalizing on it. Because if it does go lower, then there's ways to mitigate that, put yourself in the right position where you can accumulate more. That's what I would be thinking about right now.”
Pavilonis said that if we see further liquidations across financial markets, he expects to see more selling of gold as well.
“We have this rationale to buy and hold onto the metals,” he said. “I think in the long term you're going to be right. But in the short term, the thesis can be wrong, so it's time to maybe even hedge a little bit further if you haven't already.”

articles.title_orig: Iran says 4 tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Iran says 4 tankers strike mines and catch fire in Strait of Hormuz, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Iran said four tankers struck mines in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen's Houthis claimed missile strikes on Saudi Arabia, escalating pressure on two fronts as the U.S. reportedly weighs renewed military action against Tehran after Tuesday's midterm elections.
The flare-up is fueling concern among regional officials and analysts that fighting could resume around the Nov. 3 vote, even as Vice President JD Vance seeks to reopen talks with Iran.
The developments underscore the competing diplomatic and military tracks now shaping the conflict, which now in its ninth month.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three tankers caught fire after striking mines along what it called an "unauthorized southern route" near the Omani coast. Iran's army said a fourth burned east of the strait.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a small boat attaching two explosive devices to a tanker about 25 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman. The blasts sparked an engine-room fire that disabled the vessel, the agency said, adding that the crew was safe.
Separately, Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Thursday also challenged a U.S. Central Command statement that American forces had cleared mines from the primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz. The vital waterway carried about one-fifth of the world's energy supplies, and has seen traffic plummet to single-digit daily passings since the war started in late February.
"Prove the claim that the Strait of Hormuz has been cleared of mines with independent evidence, not a statement," IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said. "The reality of the Strait of Hormuz is determined in the air, on land and at sea, not on social media and in America's media war rooms."
Iran-backed Houthi forces said they launched six military operations across Saudi Arabia, targeting airports and oil facilities, despite a rare meeting of Saudi and Iranian senior officials in Tehran earlier this week. The two sides had agreed to resolve regional differences through dialogue.
Saudi authorities have not confirmed the attacks but said their air defenses have intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone launched toward the holy Mecca region.
Earlier this week, Vance sent a letter via Qatari mediators to Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing a framework for talks.
President Donald Trump, when asked whether he directed the outreach, said "no," framing it as Iran needing " help with medical supplies and various things ." "He [Vance] asked me what I thought. I said, 'if you want to do that, that's OK,'" Trump said.
Reports have emerged that the Trump administration may resume military actions in the Middle East after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Adm. Brad Cooper, top U.S. commander in the region briefed Trump on military options for Iran in a rare in-person visit to the White House, the Wall Street Journal reported late Thursday, citing unnamed U.S. officials close to the matter.
The meeting, joined by other cabinet members, covered other topics including the continuing U.S. blockade, according to the report.

A dramatic surge in military tension has taken center stage as President Trump ordered a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East – all while making cryptic claims that the standoff will soon reach its conclusion.
US Central Command confirmed that bringing three aircraft carrier strike groups into the Middle East represents the largest US naval surge in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq .
Trump voiced confidence today that the conflict would dissipate, though he provided no specific timeline or strategy for how that outcome would be secured.
'It's going to get wrapped up soon,' Trump stated during an interview with a Kansas City radio station. 'We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon.'
The remarks comes as questions surrounding Trump's domestic campaign itinerary arise, with the President rescheduling several canceled rallies over the weekend.
Vice President JD Vance also canceled a scheduled Friday press briefing in St. Cloud, Minnesota , focused on the administration's 'War on Fraud.'
Officials have not provided a reason for the cancellation.
Recent reports suggest the administration is laying the groundwork for a fresh wave of aggressive military strikes if Iranian leaders refuse to sign an agreement.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is pictured

Despite initiating the war in February expecting a rapid surrender from Iran's weakened regime, Trump has continuously maintained that the conflict will draw to a close, even while combat intensifies and global economic damage continues to mount.
This has led to voter dissatisfaction across both parties ahead of the midterm elections.
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress.
Two US officials report that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are scheduled to arrive in the Middle East by late November.
Upon arrival, the Roosevelt will operate alongside the USS George H.W. Bush, which deployed in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August as a replacement for the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Meanwhile, the nation's highest–ranking Middle East commander has reportedly briefed Trump on potential strike scenarios regarding Iran.
Admiral Brad Cooper visited the White House on Thursday with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Wall Street Journal reports.
As Trump evaluates strategy options for resuming military action against Iran, the discussion with cabinet officials included potential plans for maintaining the ongoing regional blockade.
Following a high-level White House meeting involving military leadership and Vice President Vance, Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia from his role as top strategist for the Joint Chiefs.
Sylvia's removal comes amid allegations that he leaked classified intelligence regarding the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.title_zh: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protestors and groups of police charging to disperse protestors in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_orig: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
articles.title_zh: Sam Altman says it’s better for RAM to be in a data center than on your desk
articles.content_orig:
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿
As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

articles.title_orig: G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov
articles.title_zh: G20 drops group photo as Europeans refuse to stand with Lavrov
articles.content_orig:
The United States has scrapped a traditional group photo of foreign ministers after European officials refused to be pictured alongside Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.
The move exposes deep rifts at the heart of the Group of 20 (G20), whose foreign ministers are meeting in the southern city of Atlanta in the United States for talks overshadowed by the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
“There will be no family photo featuring our European partners together with Mr Lavrov,” German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said, according to the dpa news agency.
Lavrov, who remains under Western sanctions imposed after Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine, arrived in Atlanta ahead of the talks, Russian state media reported. Moscow said on Thursday that he would use his speech to argue against international sanctions. Ukraine was not invited, the Abu Dhabi-based newspaper The National reported.
A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Russia’s presence at the G20 “in no way legitimises its actions”.
The European Union’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas pledged on Thursday to urge G20 partners to strengthen support for Ukraine and pursue accountability through a special tribunal and claims commission, after a Russian strike on a Ukrainian railway station killed at least 14 people earlier that day.
The meeting also comes weeks after US President Donald Trump issued sanctions waivers allowing Russia to export diesel to ease fuel prices before the November 3 midterm elections.
Opening the talks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged members to cooperate on economic and geopolitical crises threatening global trade, energy and food supplies, and freedom of navigation, dpa reported. Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz after US-Israeli strikes began in late February, and global energy prices have risen sharply since.
“Both maritime and food security drive economic security,” Rubio wrote on X.
No joint statement is expected. A diplomatic source told the AFP news agency that Washington will instead publish a chair’s summary it has drafted. The source added: “The G20 is no longer really a forum where foreign ministers can reach agreement on a statement.”
No government has said whether Rubio and Lavrov will hold a formal bilateral meeting.
China sent Executive Vice Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu in place of Foreign Minister Wang Yi, according to a delegation list released by the Department of State. South Africa, a founding G20 member, has been excluded by Washington, and the African Union is represented by Burundi’s Edouard Bizimana.
The Atlanta talks are the last ministerial meeting of the US G20 presidency before leaders meet in Miami on December 14 and 15.

Polish president Karol Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal on Friday as the country’s top court was thrown into chaos after its president was suspended.
Police and protesters clashed outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them. Reports suggest riot police were deployed on Friday evening as demonstrators supporting the Law and Order (PiS) party, who oppose the government, threw objects at officers.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland . I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Mr Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, said on X.
The tribunal ⁠said on its website that the court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, ​had ⁠been suspended on Friday.
A ‌long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of ‌Poland's former nationalist government of the Law ‌and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, who was a deputy ⁠justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.
Restoring the rule of law is the government's duty, prime minister Donald Tusk said on X later on Friday.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” prime minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek told ‌reporters he has requested the ⁠lifting of the immunities of Swieczkowski and his deputy ⁠for failing to fulfill their duties by preventing judges from performing their ‌work.
PiS politicians, ​including leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, said Tusk's ‌government was carrying out a ​coup on the tribunal.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
articles.title_zh: Wall Street closes sharply lower as AI cash burn fears spark tech selloff
articles.content_orig:
Tech stocks plunged Friday, erasing more than $1 trillion in value. The Nasdaq 100 index fell 3.4% in afternoon trading, its worst one-day drop since mid-June.
The sell-off pushed the Nasdaq 100 close to what is known as “correction territory,” which is a decline of 10% or more from an index’s last record high.
The broader S&P 500 also sharply dropped 1.8%. The S&P’s tech sector was by far the worst performing of the day, tumbling by more than 4.2%.
As trillion-dollar tech companies spend hundreds of billions of dollars to build out artificial intelligence data centers, investors are looking for clearer signs that all that spending is actually delivering returns.
These questions underpinned one of the day’s worst-performing stocks, Intel, which plunged 29% in its worst-ever single-day drop, according to data dating back to the 1980s.
Several of Intel’s large peers followed it lower. SanDisk plunged 13%; chipmakers AMD, ARM Holdings, Qualcomm and Marvell all fell around 10%.
The seeds of Friday’s massive losses were sown Thursday, however, when Amazon and Intel reported quarterly earnings that failed to reassure investors and analysts.
Shares of Amazon declined by as much as 10% in post-market trading Thursday, before recovering throughout the day Friday. The company’s shares ended Friday down just 1.4%.
The Philadelphia semiconductor index, of which Intel is a member, sank 7.2% on Friday. The “DRAM” ETF, which tracks companies linked to computer memory and storage, tumbled 7%.
So-called “neocloud” stocks also sold off. These upstart firms aim to build data centers for software firms to utilize. Nebius and CoreWeave dropped more than 10%.
The broader Nasdaq Composite, which tracks the more than 3,000 companies that trade on the exchange, fell 2.8%.
On Thursday, Amazon reported that its spending to build out AI had continued at a faster clip than expected last quarter, while growth in its core online shopping business had slowed.
The last time Amazon told investors it was upping its AI spending budget, the market rewarded the decision by sending shares up more than 15%.
But a lot has changed in the past three months. Some of the big companies that pay to use AI models have tightened their token budgets. Others have raised questions about exactly how much benefit they’re getting from all the time and resources they’re putting into AI adoption.
In response, some investors are now looking at Big Tech’s massive AI spending through a more skeptical lens .
Nonetheless, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told shareholders Thursday to brace for even more spending.
“We still expect 2026 cash [capital expenditures] of approximately $220 billion, the majority for AWS, and expect to spend meaningfully more in 2027,” he said on the company’s earnings call. Amazon’s spending had already been set to double from 2025.
Friday’s losses follow significant selling in shares of Alphabet on Thursday .
The Google parent company shed about $500 billion in market value — its worst day ever and the second-worst wipeout of value in market history. On Friday, the stock dropped another 1.4%.
Intel, meanwhile, told investors that its profits and sales in the fourth quarter would be lower than expected, which sent the stock tanking.
Intel’s stock has surged in recent months as its management implements a sweeping overhaul of the long-ailing chip firm.
In the midst of that turnaround, the U.S. government took a stake in the company , making the federal government the company’s largest shareholder.
Even accounting for Friday’s expected drop, the value of the government’s stake in Intel has grown by 280%.
Analysts at Citigroup described the report as “two steps forward, one step back.”
A major issue highlighted by Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan that contributed to the company’s lackluster performance in the quarter was supply chain issues.
“I’m disappointed that we were not able to meet strong customer demand in this quarter,” Tan told investors on the company’s earnings call. “We face near-term challenges, including manufacturing, supply shortage, the unprecedented memory crunch and the resulting softness in PC demand.”
Meanwhile, the sell-off in tech shares appeared to increase demand for U.S. Treasuries, which briefly sent yields on government bonds lower.
The big AI companies that are borrowing hundreds of billions for data center build-outs have tapped the debt markets for funds, which has in turn created more competition for capital.
As those companies increasingly offer better rates of return for lenders than the U.S. government does on bonds, Treasury yields have risen in recent months — partly to keep up with the private market.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: China Claims GJ-21 Naval UCAV has Flown from Type 076 Sichuan LHD
articles.title_zh: China Claims GJ-21 Naval UCAV has Flown from Type 076 Sichuan LHD
articles.content_orig:
China’s GJ-21 naval Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV) has reportedly conducted its first takeoff and landing aboard the Type 076 Sichuan amphibious assault ship, the Chinese military announced on Oct. 30, 2026 . The development was first reported by state news agencies Xinhua and Global Times , and subsequently publicized by the Ministry of National Defense and the official China Military Bugle social media account.
The military described the GJ-21 as the country’s “first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone,” saying that it “recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the ‘Sichuan’.” However, neither the state press nor the military released any official image or video of the actual flight operations.
The development comes as the U.S. Navy advances its own MQ-25 Stingray unmanned aerial refueler program. Primarily designed as a carrier-based tanker, the MQ-25 will also provide a secondary maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capability. The Stingray is expected to help mature the technologies and operational concepts needed for unmanned carrier aviation, laying the groundwork for the Navy’s future Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) fleet.
The GJ-21 has so far been associated with the Type 076, but future operations from conventional aircraft carriers have also been suggested, with speculation about the drone eventually operating from Fujian, China’s newest carrier. In our previous reports, we have assessed that the GJ-21 could provide an amphibious task group with an embarked unmanned ISR-and-strike capability, potentially extending reconnaissance and precision-attack options beyond the ship’s immediate surroundings
China’s first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone “GJ-21” recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the “Sichuan” (Hull 51).
This is another significant breakthrough in the development of China’s amphibious assault ship, indicating that the Chinese Navy now has the capability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime combat platforms.
Launched on December 27, 2024, the Sichuan (Hull 51) is the first vessel of Type 076 amphibious assault ships designed and developed independently by China. It incorporates the automatic carrier landing guidance system, new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing technology, and is capable of carrying fixed-wing unmanned aircraft, helicopters, and amphibious equipment, etc.
Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan warship has been steadily conducting various maritime tests as planned, successfully completing the debugging of various equipment and overall operational stability tests.

Unlike the US “Lightning Carrier” concept of F-35B on amphibious ships, limited by vertical takeoff payload and range, plus the risk and cost of every manned jet; the Type 076 uses electromagnetic catapults and stealth UAV swarms for higher launch rate, longer reach, better endurance and zero pilot risk.

Global Times additionally quoted Chinese military analyst Song Zongping, who described the GJ-21’s flight operations from the Sichuan as a “global first” and compared it to the U.S. Navy’s X-47B program. “[The] US X-47B carrier-based drone program was designed for aircraft carriers, yet multiple technical constraints led to its cancellation. By contrast, the GJ-21 program has advanced steadily with an efficient development timeline,” Song told GT .
However, the comparison requires some qualification: the X-47B was an experimental demonstrator that successfully completed a series of carrier-aviation milestones before the UCAS-D (Unmanned Combat Air System – Demonstrator) program concluded in 2015. The Navy subsequently redirected its follow-on unmanned-aircraft effort toward the CBARS (Carrier-Based Aerial-Refueling System) aerial-refueling role, which evolved into the MQ-25 Stingray.
Song further added that the GJ-21 may also operate from China’s other EMALS carrier, the Fujian. He argued that this would help “building the technical know-how for China’s third aircraft carrier to host manned-unmanned teaming, expanding the operational modes of carrier strike groups.”
